citation: Tu, C.-H. (2002). The measurement of social presence in an online learning environment. International Journal on E-Learning, [volume/issue ****** UNVERIFIED: not stated in extracted text], 34-45.
discipline: Educational technology / distance education (CMC social-presence measurement)
thesis: No existing instrument adequately captures the complexity of social presence in a CMC learning environment: nearly all prior studies used Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) four-item semantic-differential scale, and the sole departure (Gunawardena & Zittle 1997, ped-sec-25) remains incomplete (privacy, recipients, topics unaddressed; some items group-specific). Social presence theory was never designed for CMC and CMC's distinctive features (multiple identities, anonymity) require a purpose-built measure. The article develops and validates the Social Presence and Privacy Questionnaire (SPPQ, 59 items), finding a five-factor structure: three social-presence dimensions (social context, online communication, interactivity) plus two privacy dimensions (system privacy, feeling of privacy), weakly but significantly correlated.

sections.title: Overview of the problem
sections.summary: States the instrument-adequacy thesis; three difficulties with Short et al.'s (1976) scale (too general; semantic-differential technique invites inconsistent respondent interpretation; Gunawardena & Zittle's 1997 fix still incomplete); frames CMC as requiring its own measure distinct from the FTF/audio/CCTV contexts social presence theory was built for.

sections.title: Literature review: Social Presence
sections.summary: Surveys social presence's instructional significance (Hackman & Walker 1990; Gunawardena & Zittle 1997; Perse et al. 1992) across three developmental stages: theory emergence, application to CMC generally, and application within education specifically.

sections.title: Online Privacy sub-review
sections.summary: Reviews five privacy-adjacent constructs feeding the SPPQ's privacy subscale: feeling of privacy (Champness), illusion of privacy (Neumann 1995), risk-taking behavior (Witmer 1997), nonchalant attitude (Friedman 1990), system privacy (Kerr & Hiltz 1982).

sections.title: Existing Studies on Social Presence
sections.summary: Chronicles the three stages empirically: emergence (Champness 1972a/b; Christie 1973/1974 lab studies separating a social-presence factor from an Aesthetic Appeal factor); CMC application (Garramone, Harris & Anderson 1986; Steinfield 1986); educational application (Perse et al. 1992; Gunawardena 1995; Gunawardena & Zittle 1997).

sections.title: Weakness of Existing Studies
sections.summary: Five limitations motivating the SPPQ: (1) unclear definition; (2) inadequate instruments (Short et al. + Gunawardena & Zittle); (3) non-education samples; (4) single-CMC-system designs; (5) artificial laboratory time constraints.

sections.title: Method
sections.summary: SPPQ development (adapted from Steinfield's 1986 CMC-attitude instrument and Witmer's 1997 perceived-privacy instrument); content validation (5-expert item-objective matching panel, 3 lemon items); construct validation (N=310, exploratory factor analysis).

sections.title: Results and Discussion
sections.summary: Five-factor solution; item-level descriptive findings per factor across three CMC channels (e-mail, bulletin board, real-time discussion); social presence x privacy correlation; limitations and future-research recommendations.

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: central, re-operationalized construct; retains Short et al.'s (1976) definition as inherited starting point but resolves it empirically into three factors (social context, online communication, interactivity) via EFA on N=310

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: treated as one of social presence's own constituent factors (pleasant, immediate-reply, responsive, comfortable-with-familiar-topics), not a separate manipulated condition; narrower than an affordance-theoretic sense of agency

constructsNote: Two non-canonical (non-§3) constructs are load-bearing but not forced into §3 rows: 'online privacy' (system privacy + feeling of privacy factors) and 'measurement-instrument validity' (content/construct validation as the article's actual object of study). See .md §3 for full treatment; not represented as edges under §3 canonical labels.
conditionsNote: Strand F not required to populate the §3 media-condition axis. This source's own comparative conditions are three CMC channel types (e-mail / bulletin board / real-time discussion), not the IVR-HMD / desktop-3D / 2D axis — no media-condition axis content applies to this unit. Design is a cross-sectional instrument-validation study (N=310 in-service/pre-service teachers, 166 online / 112 paper-and-pencil), not a manipulated media-comparison experiment.

readings.claim: Short et al.'s (1976) four-item semantic-differential scale is too general for CMC and the technique itself invites inconsistent respondent interpretation of keywords.
Gunawardena & Zittle's (1997) instrument improves on Short et al. but remains incomplete: privacy, recipients, and topic variables unaddressed; some items group-specific.

Social presence theory was originally built for face-to-face, audio, and closed-circuit-television encounters, not CMC; CMC's multiple-identity and anonymity characteristics require a purpose-built measure.

Factor analysis of the SPPQ's 30 retained items yields a five-factor structure (social context, online communication, interactivity, system privacy, feeling of privacy) explaining 82.33% of variance, alpha .74-.85.
Social presence is jointly a function of media attributes (online communication), user perception (social context), and user activity/engagement (interactivity) — not media attributes alone.
The social presence x privacy correlation, r(319)=.30, p<.01, is significant but weak, leaving privacy's status as a social-presence dimension unresolved.

Respondents rate CMC as not private/not confidential yet still consider privacy important and remain willing to share personal topics — a 'controversial finding' linked to Witmer's (1997) Risk-Taking-Behavior pattern.
The SPPQ's alpha values (.74-.85) are 'medium-low' and the instrument is offered only as a first step, not a finished measure.

interlocutors.name: Short, John A., Ederyn Williams & Bruce Christie (1976)
interlocutors.role: origin theory: source of the four-item semantic-differential social-presence scale and the field's inherited definition ('degree of salience of another person'); the primary instrument Tu contests as too general for CMC

interlocutors.name: Gunawardena, Charlotte N. & Frank J. Zittle (1997) — in-cluster ped-sec-25
interlocutors.role: sole prior CMC-context alternative to Short et al.'s scale; named and critiqued directly as still incomplete (privacy, recipients, topics unaddressed; some items group-specific)

interlocutors.name: Garrison, D. Randy, Terry Anderson & Walter Archer (2000/1999) — in-cluster ped-sec-26
interlocutors.role: cited in-text (as 2000) among studies postulating social presence's potential for future study; same paper as ped-sec-26's Community-of-Inquiry source

interlocutors.name: Steinfield, Charles W. (1986)
interlocutors.role: source of the 16-item semantic-differential CMC-attitude instrument adapted (with business-specific items removed) into the SPPQ; also reviewed as an application-of-social-presence-to-CMC study (organizational e-mail use)

interlocutors.name: Witmer, Diane F. (1997) — NOT the same author as ped-sec-02's Bob G. Witmer & Michael J. Singer
interlocutors.role: source of the 32-item Likert perceived-privacy instrument adapted into the SPPQ; her 'Risk-Taking Behavior' finding (online users feel secure despite low actual privacy) is invoked to interpret Tu's own privacy results

interlocutors.name: Champness, B.G. (1972a, 1972b, 1973)
interlocutors.role: lab studies establishing the social-presence factor's separability from an 'Aesthetic Appeal' factor; also source of the 'feeling of privacy' construct

interlocutors.name: Christie, Bruce (1973, 1974)
interlocutors.role: further lab studies confirming social presence as distinct from Aesthetic Appeal and establishing text-based media (business letter) as lowest in social presence among tested media

interlocutors.name: Osgood, Charles E., George J. Suci & Percy H. Tannenbaum (1957)
interlocutors.role: originators of the semantic-differential technique underlying Short et al.'s (1976) and most prior social-presence instruments; Tu's second critique targets this technique itself

interlocutors.name: Gunawardena, Charlotte N. (1995, solo)
interlocutors.role: distance-education conferencing study cited as prior evidence that learners actively construct social presence in text-based CMC despite lacking non-verbal cues

interlocutors.name: Hackman, Michael Z. & Kathleen B. Walker (1990)
interlocutors.role: prior finding (interactive television) that system design and teacher immediacy jointly affect student learning and satisfaction, cited as precedent Gunawardena & Zittle extend to CMC

interlocutors.name: Neumann, Peter (1995)
interlocutors.role: source of the 'illusion of privacy' construct (users underestimate visibility to lurkers), incorporated into the SPPQ's privacy review

interlocutors.name: Kerr, Elaine B. & Starr Roxanne Hiltz (1982)
interlocutors.role: source of the 'system privacy' construct (concern that messages may be intercepted/reposted), incorporated into the SPPQ's system-privacy factor

tensions.axis: instrument-as-improvement (this article's own framing) vs. instrument-as-still-provisional (the article's own stated limitations)
tensions.note: Tu positions the SPPQ as a corrective to Short et al. (1976) and Gunawardena & Zittle (1997), yet closes by conceding medium-low reliability (alpha .74-.85) and calling the SPPQ only 'a first step' — an internal tension the article does not resolve.

tensions.axis: social presence as media-attribute-driven (technology-determinist) vs. social presence as jointly determined by media, perception, and activity/engagement
tensions.note: Tu explicitly rejects a purely media-attribute account, arguing interactivity (user activity/engagement) is empirically separable and co-determining — directly relevant to any Part III claim that media condition alone explains presence differences.

tensions.axis: privacy as a genuine social-presence dimension vs. privacy as a merely correlated, separable construct
tensions.note: The significant-but-weak r=.30 correlation leaves this open; Tu declines to claim privacy belongs inside social presence proper, unlike his confident claim about interactivity.

bridgeNote: vle-01's survey instrument, insofar as it elicits student-reported perceived social/co-presence with peers, sits downstream of exactly the measurement lineage this article critiques and extends; useful for flagging that 'social presence' as a self-report construct has an unsettled, still-being-revised operational history rather than one canonical scale. Tu's finding that social presence is jointly determined by media, perception, and activity/engagement (not media alone) offers a citable argumentative structure — not a directly transferable numeric result, since Tu's conditions are CMC channels, not spatial/immersive media — for resisting a purely technology-determinist reading of media-condition differences in Part III's own findings.
